summaries.title: Note Overview
summaries.gist: An informal note by Chris Olah, published May 4 2023, sets out to explain how superposition relates to distributed representations.

summaries.title: Distributed Representations: Composition & Superposition
summaries.gist: Distributed representations blend two separable strategies, composition and superposition, shown through four example neural codes ranging from one neuron per stimulus to dense, maximally superposed codes.
summaries.question: Distributed representations — how do composition and superposition differ across Thorpe's example codes? (four examples)

summaries.title: Framing Distributed Representations
summaries.gist: Distributed representations are often treated as one idea, but the article argues they actually combine two separable notions, composition and superposition, illustrated using Thorpe's four neuron codes for colored shapes.

summaries.title: "Local" Codes
summaries.gist: In Thorpe's local code each neuron represents one specific color-shape pair with no superposition, letting future layers linearly select any combination of stimuli, though it uses many neurons.

summaries.title: "Semi-Local" / Compositional Codes
summaries.gist: The semi-local or compositional code uses separate neurons for color and shape that combine to represent objects, needing far fewer neurons and generalizing to new combinations, while staying easy to interpret.

summaries.title: "Dense" / Maximal Superposition Codes
summaries.gist: A dense, maximally superposed code needs only four neurons to represent all sixteen colored shapes, but linear probes can no longer cleanly read out individual colors or shapes.

summaries.title: Composition vs Superposition
summaries.gist: Though the example codes look like one spectrum from local to distributed, composition and superposition are actually two competing strategies for allocating a fixed exponential encoding space.
summaries.question: Composition and superposition — why are they competing strategies rather than points on one spectrum? (a formal argument)

summaries.title: Two Orthogonal Strategies
summaries.gist: Although the three codes look like points on one spectrum from local to distributed, the semi-local and highly-distributed codes actually follow two distinct, independent strategies, composition and superposition.

summaries.title: Allocating Exponential Volume
summaries.gist: With a fixed number of bits, composable features can only fill a small share of possible states, while non-composing features can fill it exponentially via superposition, though retrieval then needs a nonlinearity.

summaries.title: Why Distinguish Them
summaries.gist: Because composition and superposition trade off distinct benefits, non-local generalization versus representing more features than neurons, treating them as one phenomenon obscures why representations sometimes fail to deliver both.

summaries.title: Mixing Composition and Superposition
summaries.gist: Composition and superposition can be combined despite competing, because sparse, rarely-co-occurring features leave gaps in compositional space that superposition can fill, as Thorpe's semi-distributed code shows.
summaries.question: Mixing the two — how can composition and superposition coexist in one representation? (a worked example)

summaries.title: Sparse Features Enable Superposition
summaries.gist: Composition and superposition seem to compete, but when features are sparse, rarely co-occurring, unused regions of the compositional space open up as gaps that can store additional features in superposition.

summaries.title: Semi-Distributed Code Example
summaries.gist: Thorpe's semi-distributed code composes color and shape features while placing colors in mutual superposition and shapes in mutual superposition, so single neurons look polysemantic though directions still encode composable features.

summaries.title: Two Codes in Tension
summaries.gist: Superposition and composition are distinct, trading-off strategies within distributed representations, and only the compositional kind lets researchers understand networks without exponential effort.
summaries.question: Why does this distinction matter — what follows for understanding neural networks? (two claims)

summaries.title: Two Kinds of Distribution
summaries.gist: Distributed representations actually name two different, competing phenomena, superposition and composition, that can be mixed somewhat but trade off because they have fundamentally different properties.

summaries.title: Why Structure Matters
summaries.gist: Because composable representations can be understood using only a linear number of independent features rather than exponential volume, recognizing composition is essential to truly reverse-engineering neural networks.

glossary.name: Superposition
glossary.senseHere: Packing more features into a representation than there are neurons, by letting neurons each respond to several unrelated (color, shape) combinations at once. This only works when a nonlinearity is available to disentangle the overlapping signals, and it sacrifices the ability to read off any single feature with a simple linear probe.

glossary.name: Composition
glossary.senseHere: Building representations of whole objects by combining separate, independent feature directions, such as a color direction and a shape direction added together to represent a colored shape. This lets a small number of features generate an exponentially larger number of combinations while staying easy to interpret piece by piece.

glossary.name: Thorpe (1989)
glossary.background: A paper by neuroscientist Simon Thorpe that laid out example neural codes ranging from 'local' to 'highly distributed' to illustrate different ways a population of neurons could represent stimuli.

glossary.name: Monosemantic
glossary.senseHere: Describes a neuron that responds to only one specific thing, such as one neuron firing only for red circles and nothing else, with no overlap or ambiguity in what it represents.

glossary.name: Linear probe
glossary.senseHere: A simple straight-line (linear) function built on top of a set of neurons to test whether some property, like 'redness,' can be read out from their activity, without needing any extra nonlinear processing.

glossary.name: Toy Models of Superposition
glossary.background: An earlier paper by the same research group studying how neural networks pack more features than they have neurons for, describing this trade-off in terms of how rarely features co-occur (their sparsity).
